knowledge.question: Should I make a separate shipping profile for big items?
knowledge.answer: Levi usually doesn't. If you switch big items to a large profile, everyone sees a new shipping charge (like $9.21) that doesn't bundle, and they bid less because they're thinking about shipping. Instead he runs big items under his small-item profile, so buyers who already have free shipping, plus first-time buyers paying $5, all compete for the item. A bigger buyer pool means higher bids.

knowledge.question: How does running big items under the small shipping profile still make money?
knowledge.answer: Levi's example was scooters that weigh about 8 lb and cost him $3 each. They sold for $25 under the small profile, so buyers were thinking only about the bid. When a first-time buyer had paid $5 shipping, he covered the remaining $5 to $10 himself. Even after paying $10 in shipping he had about $15 left before fees, which beat the roughly $10 he'd have gotten if buyers were scared off by a separate shipping charge.

knowledge.question: How do I unbundle a big item after the label is already created?
knowledge.answer: You can still edit a bundle after generating the label. On your laptop, go to Shipments, open that bundle, click the little pen icon, choose unbundle shipment, and select the item, like the scooter. Then set it to its correct weight and pay the shipping difference. Levi's shippers do this when an item gets to the shipping station and is obviously too big or heavy for the box.

knowledge.question: When should I NOT pay shipping out of pocket on big items?
knowledge.answer: Levi says this works best if you have about 80 to 150, even 200, viewers, where your buyers care about shipping cost. Sellers with 250+ or 800+ viewers don't need it because they make money on lots of first-time buyers who don't care about shipping. Skip it if the item is so big that shipping will be insane, or if you only have about 20 viewers and the item won't go for retail. He uses it for items that go for about $20 to $30 and usually sell high.

knowledge.question: Why do people buy on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi believes people buy on Whatnot for three reasons: the streamer (the host), the inventory, and free shipping. On Amazon free shipping is baked into prices, but on Whatnot the buyer pays shipping, so anything that removes shipping worry gets people bidding more. His shows have about a 50% returning buyer rate daily because buyers love the bundles, the streamers and the inventory.

knowledge.question: Where in the show should I run big items?
knowledge.answer: Levi's team sells about 500 items per show and throws the big items in after around item 250 or 300, or even at the end. By then lots of viewers have bought more than two items and already have free shipping, so more people compete for the big item. He also says light-up scooters do very well on Whatnot because they don't cost much in store but have a lot of perceived value in an auction.

knowledge.question: Does my background matter on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Yes, especially as a beginner. People are constantly swiping through shows, and your background is the first impression: if they see something good in it, they zoom in and stay. Levi says the top streamers show their face and have prizes in the background. As a beginner you need to do everything possible to raise the chance people stay and bid.

knowledge.question: What items should I put in my Whatnot background?
knowledge.answer: Put items that are either high-ticket or that people are actively looking for, because they increase bids. Levi's example is Wagyu hats, which sell for about $18 on average in his shows, retail for $35, and cost him around 7-8% of retail. If you have a rare item from your pallets, put it in the background to build anticipation. Even faceless sellers should have a very nice background, with as many as 100 different items people will wait for.

knowledge.question: Should I do faceless shows or show my face?
knowledge.answer: Levi knows faceless sellers who do very well, but one of his students doing faceless wasn't getting results. He told him he had the personality for it and to show himself on camera with a background, since he'd most likely do much better. The top streamers on Whatnot show their face.

knowledge.question: How do I let buyers know I have a hot item in stock without announcing it?
knowledge.answer: Levi doesn't do listings; he does random pulls. When a popular item like Wagyu hats comes in, he puts about 10 in the background. Buyers who want them see them while swiping, stay in the show, and new customers who like them stay too. You can't see who's watching, but the background calls them in.

knowledge.question: When should I run the best items in my show?
knowledge.answer: Levi builds anticipation by running the best items later. His streams average 7 hours, so he'll run the hot item around 3 hours in, dropping one here and there earlier to show he will sell them. Some buyers wait the whole stream, even 6 hours, to put in their max bid. While they wait, they swipe and buy other items, pushing up prices for everyone, which helps the entire show.

knowledge.question: Are Whatnot buyers just looking for cheap stuff?
knowledge.answer: Levi says that's not true. People have sold $1,800 and $1,000 items to his customers, and he sells expensive items starting at $1, with an average show price around $68 on a fair day. People will pay for the right items, so give your viewers the good stuff.

knowledge.question: Why should I follow back my top buyers on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi follows back all his silver, gold, platinum and diamond rewards members (diamond in his show means over $2,000 spent in a 3-month rewards season). About 250-300 people in those tiers make up half of his revenue in a season. When you follow them, unless they have private entry turned on, you get notified when they join your show, so you can pull out the products you know they like. Some of his biggest buyers never say a word; he calls them silent killers.

knowledge.question: Why include silver-tier buyers and not just the top spenders?
knowledge.answer: Levi has seen buyers go from spending about $300 as silver members in one season to $2,000 in the next and stay at that level every season. He credits customer trust and changing inventory. That's why he follows back from silver up, not just diamond, but skips bronze since it's very easy to hit.

knowledge.question: How do I estimate how much profit a Whatnot show actually makes?
knowledge.answer: Levi's quick method: take about 85% of the show's sales to account for fees, then divide by the number of units sold to get what you keep per unit. In his example, with average fees the seller makes about $2 profit per unit, which works out to roughly $6K profit in a 7-hour show. His point is that people who say Whatnot is dead just don't know how to run the numbers.

knowledge.question: How fast can I grow a $10K inventory investment?
knowledge.answer: Levi's conservative math: buy $10K of inventory, sell through all of it in your first week, and make $5K profit (a 50% return), so you have $15K. Reinvest it and make $7,500, bringing you to $22.5K after week two. Do it again and you're around $33K, and after one more week of selling everything you could reach about $45K in your first month. The key is being committed to selling through your whole inventory each week, and payouts come fast, about 4 hours after delivery, or the same night once you unlock instant payouts.

knowledge.question: Does the platform I sell on change how many packages I have to ship?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi sold the same inventory on both platforms: one show produced 175 packages, while the other produced only 70 packages from 450 units. He estimates that even if the second show had sold the full 600 units it probably wouldn't have passed 90 shipments, so roughly half the packages. Fewer, bigger bundles mean much less packing work for your shipping team.

knowledge.question: Do I need to do product research or ungating before selling live?
knowledge.answer: Levi says no. His model is simply buy low, sell high: there's a ton of product you can get very cheap, and that's what they do, with no ungating and no product research up front. Your product research happens on the live, where you see what sells. He adds that they also bought outside the box, and it's all legal; otherwise they wouldn't be allowed on TikTok and Whatnot or invited to big trade shows.

knowledge.question: Do I need as much capital for live selling as for Amazon?
knowledge.answer: No. Levi says big Amazon sellers do around $2-3 million in sales to reach 100K-profit months, and his team does more than $100K profit months without putting in that much capital. Live sellers work with 30% up to 70-80% profit margins, and Levi personally runs around 40% while doing volume. You control your margins and your sales because you're selling an item every 10-30 seconds, which is why he calls live selling roughly 10x compared to Amazon.

knowledge.question: How do I scale my live selling profit?
knowledge.answer: Hire another streamer. Levi's conservative math: if a streamer makes $1 net profit per unit and sells 600 units a shift, that's $600 per shift, about $3,000 a week and roughly $12,000 net profit a month. So each additional person you hire can add about $12K a month in net profit, which is more than the average salary. It's a volume game.

knowledge.question: Should I go live myself or hire a streamer from the start?
knowledge.answer: Try it yourself first, at least once or twice, before asking anyone for help. Levi says if you don't want to be on camera and don't have the capital to hire someone, live selling probably isn't for you. If you do have the capital, hire, but only when the numbers make sense. He hired very quickly, not because he avoids the camera (he's done hundreds or thousands of hours live) but because doing it all yourself isn't scalable; manage from the outside and grow it.

knowledge.question: What equipment do I need to start selling on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says you can really run the whole business with one phone, but to move fast he recommends a tripod, good lighting, a scale, the phone for the camera, and another phone, laptop or iPad to start the auctions. For shipping you need a laptop, a thermal printer, tape, bubble wrap and poly bags.

knowledge.question: Why should I organize my inventory shelves by weight?
knowledge.answer: Levi categorizes each shelf by weight: 1 to 3 oz, 4 to 7 oz, 8 to 11 oz, and 12 to 15 oz. Hosts weigh the product and start the auction under the matching weight, which offers buyers the right shipping price. This supports bundle shipping, which increases retention because buyers stay to lower their shipping cost per unit.

knowledge.question: What should I start my auction bids at?
knowledge.answer: Start the bid at whatever you're comfortable selling at. Levi won't start a $200 product at $1 if he isn't pulling 200 viewers yet; he might start it at $30 or $60 depending on how many viewers are there. If an item doesn't sell, run it again in 20 or 30 minutes, because with 19 viewers now and 80 later, someone will pay your price.

knowledge.question: How does viewer count affect pricing on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says it's a numbers game: with 20 viewers you might have one person interested in a product, but with 100 viewers you might have five. When you know several people will compete, you can start the bid lower because the bidding will go up.

knowledge.question: Why does bundle shipping keep buyers in my show?
knowledge.answer: Whatnot has a $9.21 flat rate up to 70 lbs in its small, medium or large flat rate boxes through its USPS contract, so you can send 20 items in one box if they fit. One item costs $9.21 to ship, but 10 items lowers the shipping per unit, so customers stay longer to keep buying. Not every seller offers bundle shipping, but Levi does to build a customer experience that raises retention.

knowledge.question: How long and how often should my live shows be?
knowledge.answer: Levi's shows run 7 to 8 hours, and night hosts may go 9 to 10 hours up to 1 or 2 a.m., which he calls prime times. The key is to be consistent with the times you're live, because customers learn your schedule; his electronics host has regulars who only come Thursday to Sunday mornings, 7:30 a.m. to 3 p.m.

knowledge.question: How should I split jobs between hosts, helpers and shippers?
knowledge.answer: In Levi's setup a helper stocks the shelves, and the host grabs, displays, weighs, talks about and promotes each product and starts the bid. Shipping happens in a separate room because shippers can't be distracted and must make sure every order goes out correctly. After each show a shipper ships everything to keep 24-hour processing time; one shipper cleared a full beauty show in 4 to 5 hours, then spent the rest of the shift prepping and stocking.

knowledge.question: What if a buyer says an item arrived damaged when I sold it as damaged?
knowledge.answer: Whatnot keeps a video receipt of what you sold in each auction or random pull. If you said on the stream that the item was damaged and sold it at a discount, the video shows the exact condition, so Whatnot has your back. Levi says customers will still pay $1–$2 for usable open-box items that retail for $10.

knowledge.question: How do I set up a show for small items like health and beauty?
knowledge.answer: Levi uses a different, faceless setup: a light box with the camera placed right on the product and the scale, while the host sets up bundles and talks in the background. Small items aren't visible if the camera is far away like in an electronics show, so you'd get fewer bids. He also adds eye-catching premium products in the background for retention and runs bundles and random pulls with quick 10-second runs instead of listing everything.

knowledge.question: Where should I place the camera for bigger items?
knowledge.answer: For bigger items like electronics, Levi puts the camera farther back behind the scale so viewers can see the whole product. If you're selling something like Dysons all day, you can have your face and whole body in the shot with the scale.

knowledge.question: Can I really make money my first day on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi started after being banned on eBay with $100,000 of inventory to move. He downloaded Whatnot, went live around 2 p.m. on a random Friday, and did $2,000 his first day. In four weeks he had 11,000 followers, $50,000 in sales and 3,500 items sold.

knowledge.question: Why choose Whatnot over Amazon or eBay?
knowledge.answer: Levi left Amazon after doing $4 million in three years, and eBay banned two of his accounts while he sold brands like Razer, Logitech and Apple. On Amazon you fight brand ungating and can be removed from listings, which means fee after fee. He says Whatnot's fees are direct, with no returns, no cancellations and no ungating. Aside from restricted categories (like coins, pallets and luxury handbags) and anything illegal or counterfeit, you can sell pretty much whatever you like.

knowledge.question: Can I move large volume of one product on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi says when he buys 1,000 units of one product he can sell out in about a week on Whatnot. He sold 1,000 Altec speakers in one week, which he says you can't do on eBay or Amazon. That volume is how someone young can break into the liquidation industry.

knowledge.question: Should I promote my Instagram or YouTube during my Whatnot shows?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi says it's within the terms of service to tell viewers your social media accounts, and you should treat Whatnot like a social media platform since you're showing your face for hours every day. His personal brand grew 5x in 9 months, his store has 160,000 followers after 10 months, and buyers reach out on Instagram wanting to buy larger quantities because they trust him. He says it's the best long-term way to collect customer data.

knowledge.question: What profit margin should I aim for on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says Amazon margins are around 15% at most, while on Whatnot you're dealing with 50% margins and up. Your actual margin depends on how you structure labor, rent and overhead, but it should be higher than 30%.

knowledge.question: How much space do I need to run a Whatnot business efficiently?
knowledge.answer: Levi says you need space to work efficiently or you lose money on labor. He started in a 200-250 sq ft storage unit and grew to 10 storage units, which was very inefficient because inventory was spread out and he didn't know what was in the back for weeks or months. He waited six months for a warehouse five minutes from home at a good price, and says sometimes it's worth waiting for the right space.

knowledge.question: Why are Whatnot instant payouts so useful?
knowledge.answer: Levi calls instant payouts magic once you unlock them after reaching enough sales. Sales from Sunday through Thursday land in your bank that same night, so you can immediately call a supplier and reinvest, for example in $40,000 of inventory. Suppliers love that, and it builds relationships you can't build on other platforms.

knowledge.question: Is it still early to start selling on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says yes. There are only about 80 sellers a day in electronics, and he believes Whatnot grew about 100% year over year in 2024 and 2025 and will again in 2026. He says live social shopping is a half-trillion-dollar market in China (about 60% of online sales there), while the US is still in the discovery phase. Buyers already spend around 90 minutes a day on the app.

knowledge.question: Should I take out a loan to start live selling?
knowledge.answer: Levi says no: if you have $10K to put into inventory, that's all you need. That gets you roughly 5,000 units, which you should be able to sell within a week, and even at a 50% ROI that's about $5K profit in your first week. It should go up every week as your systems get more efficient, you learn to sell better and your account grows. Once you unlock instant payouts you get paid quickly, so you scale from there using the same money. He compares this to an Amazon seller doing $100K a month in sales and making around $17K profit, which isn't even net or take-home.

knowledge.question: How many items should I have for my first Whatnot shows?
knowledge.answer: Levi recommends starting with 100 items; if you don't have inventory, you can start by selling what's in your house. Whatnot sends a lot of traffic to new sellers' first few shows to show proof of concept. His first weekend, three streams did $8,000 in sales using a liquidation pallet he already had for eBay.

knowledge.question: How do I find a reliable liquidation supplier?
knowledge.answer: Levi says there are liquidators all over the US. Call ahead to ask what they have in stock, then drive there and meet them in person. Smaller liquidators may not get much supply and can run out of stock, so find someone you can rely on to buy from consistently. He likes liquidation because you're buying under 20% of retail.

knowledge.question: What are the main reasons people buy on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says people buy on Whatnot for three reasons: the inventory, the streamer, and free shipping. Buyers aren't buying things they really need, since they'd pay retail for those; they buy what they want because it's a bargain.

knowledge.question: Should I sell high-ticket or low-ticket items as a beginner?
knowledge.answer: Levi recommends low-ticket items. High ticket, like electronics, is harder to source consistently, costs more (roughly 25-50% of retail), and shrinks your buyer pool because not everyone has $100 to spend on a random day. Employee streamers also don't push for top dollar the way an owner does. He focuses on good-quality low-ticket goods, like Target products, bought at liquidation prices so he can give everyone a bargain. As a rough target, if an item retails for $100, aim to get about $40 for it.

knowledge.question: What should I do when my liquidation pallet arrives?
knowledge.answer: Take everything out of the pallet and sort it. Levi wishes he'd done this from the start: they used to sell from the top of pallets, where the best items were, and were left with only okay items like goggles and hats at the bottom. Sorting lets you find multiples and the good stuff at the bottom so you can blend items properly into your shows.

knowledge.question: What should I do if an item sells for way less than I wanted?
knowledge.answer: Don't immediately rerun it hoping for more. Levi says the biggest mistake he sees is selling something for $2 when you wanted $6, complaining that chat is sleeping, and running it again right away; if it just sold for $2, it will likely sell for $1 next. Low prices usually mean the buyers who wanted it are gone. On the other hand, if an item that usually averages $5 suddenly sells for $20, run it again and again until it drops back to its average.

knowledge.question: How do I use free shipping to raise prices during a show?
knowledge.answer: Levi's offer is 'buy two, get the next eight free shipping.' If you start at $1, expect the first 30-40 items to go low, but keep reminding people about free shipping. Once those first buyers have free shipping, they compete to fill their bundles and prices go up, while new people keep entering and trying to fill theirs. When things slow down around 300 items, announce an end point, like ending at 1:00 p.m. or having 100 items left, and buyers rush to fill their boxes.

knowledge.question: Should I use $1 starts or $5 starts on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says $1 starts get people moving and work best for long shows (his main shows can go up to 500 items) where free shipping drives the bidding. For shorter shows of 50-100 items, use starting prices; on a new account doing only 100 items per show with $5 starts, his pricing is much higher. With $5 starts, results depend heavily on the streamer and the product rather than free shipping.

knowledge.question: How should I treat buyers during my show?
knowledge.answer: Levi says be happy people are there and don't complain about pricing. Thank every single buyer, and when someone makes a first purchase, say 'thank you for your first purchase.' Recognize regulars by name when they pop in or swipe ('I see you!') so they feel welcome. Pay attention to what each buyer buys, like who's a reseller or who has lots of kids, especially if your inventory is consistent.

knowledge.question: Do giveaways really help on Whatnot, and what should I give away?
knowledge.answer: Levi says giveaways are part of the algorithm and drive traffic: there's a spike of viewers in the last 30 seconds of every giveaway. On one slow 10-viewer night, his streamer ran giveaways back-to-back and viewers snowballed from 20 to 30, 40, then 50. Even if only three of those 50 people buy, they're buyers you'd never have found. His team ran 9,000 giveaways in three months, and they were all stickers. Expect some 'giveaway goblins' to leave bad reviews; it's still worth it.

knowledge.question: What do I need for a basic Whatnot show setup?
knowledge.answer: Keep it simple: a phone to run the auction, a ring light and some lighting, and a second phone, which can be an old one. Levi says a background of products matters for beginners because it shows what you have, and putting high-ticket items on the shelves makes them sell for more because several bidders wait for them. At the start of a show, show viewers everything you're running so they know they can fill their boxes.

knowledge.question: How should I schedule my Whatnot shows?
knowledge.answer: Always have upcoming shows listed, even with the same thumbnail, so buyers can bookmark them; you can reschedule if needed. Be consistent with your times: Levi's accounts go live from 6:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. every day, so buyers know when to show up. Pro tip: upload your listings into one show, then clone them into other shows.

knowledge.question: What is the numbered sticker system for tracking sold items?
knowledge.answer: Levi asked ChatGPT to create a PDF for a thermal printer with 2x1 labels numbered 1 to 2,000 and prints the range he needs for each show. Each item that sells gets the next number, so a finished show is tagged in order. If you're running item 50 and the sticker says 51, you know something went wrong (a printer skip or a lost sticker) and can find the mistake quickly.

knowledge.question: How should I set up shipping profiles and boxes on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Find your average product weight; for Levi it's 15 oz, about five items per Priority Mail box. Make a shipping profile at 15 oz with a max of five per bundle (75 oz) so the first item doesn't carry the full box cost. Set buyer pays shipping, include first class, USPS Priority Mail, and Priority Mail flat rate so you can downgrade to flat rate if needed, and use the default 12x12x12 size. He mostly uses one large box size, an 18x12x8 box with the same 1,728 cubic inches, and remembers that a flat rate box must carry a matching flat rate label.

knowledge.question: How do I drop off lots of Whatnot packages at USPS without each one being scanned?
knowledge.answer: Generate a USPS scan sheet in the Whatnot shipments tab right after you generate your labels, the same day; you can't do it the next day. Levi says the app often glitches, so use Whatnot in Chrome on a laptop: shipments tab, open the sidebar, generate the scan sheet. Give it to the post office and all your packages are scanned in at once, so you're on time instead of waiting days for the first scan. At higher volume, schedule a commercial pickup by calling USPS corporate.

knowledge.question: Is TikTok Live Auction good for beginners?
knowledge.answer: Levi says TikTok Live Auction is not beginner-friendly if you don't have a rep. There are violations almost every day for random things; his account got one on day one for selling too low, even though auctions naturally go low. Without a rep to clear violations, TikTok can limit your account, payouts and daily orders. New accounts are capped at around 5-10 items a day, and his appeal with business verification was still rejected by their AI, so it took him 4 weeks to get his accounts onboarded.

knowledge.question: How do I get a TikTok Shop rep?
knowledge.answer: Levi says TikTok reps make commission off your sales, so they want to work with sellers already doing over $100,000 a month on Whatnot. A rep helps push appeals through and clear violations from the AI, which is a huge advantage on TikTok. That's why he recommends building on Whatnot first if you're a beginner.

knowledge.question: How fast can I start selling on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: You can start selling the same day you sign up. Levi downloaded the app at 5 a.m., scheduled his live for 1 p.m. and was live at 2. He sold roughly 200 items his first day and did $8,000 over three days. On Whatnot you can sell 1,000 or even 10,000 items on your first day, compared to the 5-10 item daily limit new TikTok sellers can face.

knowledge.question: How do I qualify for instant payouts on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi lists the requirements as $1,000 in sales or 1,000 units sold, a 4.8 rating and at least 10 shows. He says 10 shows is easy: you can restart your live 10 times in one day, then wait for an order to deliver to get your rating. Once you have instant payouts, if you cash out before about 3:30-4 p.m. the money is in your bank that night.

knowledge.question: Why are instant payouts so important on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi calls instant payouts where the magic is. With $1,000 and a local supplier, you can buy product, sell out today, get paid tonight and go back to the supplier the next morning to spend it again, recycling the same capital every day. Note the weekly schedule: the cutoff is Thursday around 4 p.m., and payouts don't restart until Sunday night, so instant payouts run Sunday through Thursday.

knowledge.question: Should I sell on TikTok Live or Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi's top recommendation is to do both and scale on both. TikTok has tons of free traffic and higher profit margins, and you don't need much skill because if you show the product it sells. Whatnot takes more strategy and has less viewership for now, but it's growing fast and competition is dropping as sellers chase TikTok. If TikTok shuts you down, you still have Whatnot.

knowledge.question: Is Whatnot getting too competitive?
knowledge.answer: Levi says the opposite: over the last 12 months competition on Whatnot has gone down because some sellers left for TikTok, while viewership has gone up 4x. Many who left weren't building a business with multiple streamers. He thinks the algorithm will favor sellers who stayed, and that bigger accounts will be rewarded as the app keeps growing.

knowledge.question: How long does it take to get 100 viewers on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: When Levi started, he went into other sellers' lives and asked how long they'd been selling; one with 100 viewers said about 8 months. His own account got to 100 viewers consistently in its fourth month, and he was making good money even before that. His advice is to be consistent, either by going live yourself or by hiring people to go live for you.

knowledge.question: Can I make money on Whatnot selling cheap items?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi's average sale is around $12 and auctions can go low, but he's profitable because he buys items for $1 to $3 or even under $1, like keychains. He planned a series selling dumplings from a supplier with plenty of stock, spending $10,000 on three days of inventory at about 100% ROI and reinvesting that same $10,000 over and over.

knowledge.question: How important is the circle of people I surround myself with as a seller?
knowledge.answer: Very important, according to Levi. He says to hang out with people who make money, because those are the circles you want to be in, and his circle runs on trust. As an example, a seller he met in Bali 10x'd by the time they met again a year later. His brother, who graduated high school in 2025, did seven figures on TikTok in his first four months at 19.

knowledge.question: How should I prepare before my first Whatnot show?
knowledge.answer: Watch other streamers before you go live, even just for a week. Levi tells his students to go on the app and study other people so they pick up the terminology and phrases. He trains his own streamers the same way: they stand behind the scenes for a couple of streams, helping out and listening to how the team talks to the community and what tactics they use.

knowledge.question: What should I say on stream to get people to buy more?
knowledge.answer: Levi's team uses lines like telling viewers the first 50 items go the cheapest every time so don't miss out, telling them items are bundled to save on shipping, and near the end of the show reminding them to fill up their bundles while they have free shipping. He says that last push creates a spike, and the ending is one of the best parts of the show when there are still 100 viewers with free shipping. Many new buyers don't know they get free shipping after a certain number of items, so tell them.

knowledge.question: Do I need a warehouse to start selling on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: No. Levi started in a 150 sq ft storage unit with two pallets, a table and maybe a display rack. He and Chase agree that sellers who rush into warehouses often aren't profitable the first few months, while starting small means you'll be making profit. Start with what's obtainable for you and scale up; going $5-10K into debt isn't worth it.

knowledge.question: Should I sell shoes and clothing on Whatnot as a beginner?
knowledge.answer: Levi says shoes and clothing are among the hardest categories, especially starting at $1. With only 50 viewers, the chance someone wants that one product in that size and style is low. Categories like consumer electronics give you a bigger buyer pool.

knowledge.question: Is it better to sell low-ticket or high-ticket items on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says margins are much higher on low-ticket items because it's an auction starting at $1. If you buy at 5-15% of retail on a $100 item, you're trying to get someone to spend $70 to hit 70% of retail, which is hard on Whatnot. You have a much better chance of getting 80% of retail on a $10 product.

lessons.title: How I Sell BIG Items on Whatnot Without Killing My Profit (Shipping Hack)
lessons.description: Levi explains why he runs big items (like 8 lb scooters) under his small-item shipping profile instead of a separate large profile, so buyers who already have free shipping keep bidding. He covers how to unbundle those items in Shipments after the show, pay the extra shipping himself, and which viewer counts and item prices this strategy fits.

lessons.title: Does Your Whatnot Background Matter? (YES… Here's Why)
lessons.description: Levi explains why your background is the first impression for viewers swiping through Whatnot, and how to fill it with high-demand or high-ticket items to keep people watching and build anticipation. He also shares how to use background items to signal new stock without announcing it, and a pro tip to follow back your top rewards-tier buyers so you see when they join.

lessons.title: Selling on Whatnot FULL Setup (Beginner Guide)
lessons.description: Levi tours his storage-unit Whatnot operation, showing the equipment for a live show and shipping station, shelves organized by weight category for bundle shipping, and how hosts start auctions. He explains pricing based on viewer count, consistent show schedules, video receipts for disputes, and a separate close-up faceless setup for small health and beauty items.

lessons.title: Why Whatnot Is the Best Platform to Sell On in 2026
lessons.description: Levi, a former Amazon seller who did $4M over three years, explains why he thinks Whatnot is the best platform in 2026 for growing your personal brand, store brand and capital. He compares fees, brand restrictions, margins and volume with Amazon and eBay, and covers driving buyers to your socials, warehouse space, instant payouts, and why live shopping is still early.

lessons.title: Whatnot Seller Course – How I Made $1.2M in 9 Months
lessons.description: Levi walks through his full Whatnot playbook from $1.2M in sales in 9 months: starting with about 100 items, sourcing liquidation, pricing and free-shipping strategy, $1 vs $5 starts, giveaways, show setup, and buyer engagement. He also covers his numbered-sticker system, shipping profiles and box sizes, packing, and using a USPS scan sheet.

lessons.title: Should You Sell on TikTok Live or Whatnot in 2026?
lessons.description: Levi compares TikTok Live Auction and Whatnot: TikTok has huge traffic and higher margins but is strict, with daily violations, onboarding limits and appeals that are hard to clear without a rep. Whatnot is beginner-friendly, lets you start selling on day one and has instant payouts. His recommendation is to build on both, and not to abandon Whatnot.

lessons.title: How to Start a Whatnot Business in 2026 (Step-by-Step)
lessons.description: Levi interviews Chase, an 18-year-old from Iowa who built a faceless six-figure Whatnot business from his family's garage while in college. They cover starting small without a warehouse, studying other streamers, picking low-cost items, testing products in small quantities from local suppliers, the best days to go live, free USPS supplies, and avoiding pallet scams.

lessons.title: Your First Whatnot Sale Explained — Shipping, Labels & Getting Paid
lessons.description: Levi walks through Whatnot's Shipments back end after a sale: when you get paid, video receipts, generating labels, switching to a large flat rate box for free, label adjustments and allowances, unbundling, and why USPS scan sheets protect your account health. He also explains small/medium/large and fill-a-box shipping profiles, the priority mail settings he recommends, and why you should never edit shipping profiles during a live show.

lessons.title: The Warehouse Setup Behind $2M in Live Auction Sales
lessons.description: Levi gives a tour of his reorganized warehouse: open floor space for shipping, racks against the wall, and all inventory moved off pallets and onto rolling racks so streamers can see and run products faster. He also explains how he handled a backpack supply drought by sourcing 40-cent keychains and bundling them for big margins.

lessons.title: Why I Left Amazon for Whatnot
lessons.description: In a short interview, Levi explains he left Amazon because of gating restrictions and rising fees, while Whatnot lets him sell liquidation and closeouts freely. He shares that he did $3,000 on his first Whatnot live with no big following and that consistency is the key tip for beginners.

lessons.title: How To Find Inventory For Whatnot (Beginner's Guide 2026)
lessons.description: Levi covers his three main ways to source Whatnot inventory (Facebook liquidation groups, trade shows, and eventually China), how to avoid supplier scams, and why beginners should start with a local liquidation pallet. He explains why a wide mix of products matters more than depth, how to calculate your true per-unit cost, and why testing products builds the data to buy big later.

lessons.title: New Whatnot Business Model Nobody Is Talking About
lessons.description: Levi describes a Whatnot business model where sellers focus only on selling while a separate fulfillment team holds the stock and ships orders, letting hosts stream from anywhere. He compares Whatnot margins to Amazon FBA, explains why the platform is still early, and shares a shipping-weight trick and software idea for more accurate postage.

lessons.title: Best Category to Sell on Whatnot for Beginners (Low Risk Strategy)
lessons.description: Levi recommends health and beauty as the best low-risk Whatnot category for beginners because liquidation stock is plentiful and cheap, products are small and light, and buyers get locked into shows filling bundles. He explains his 'buy two, get the next eight free' custom shipping profile, flat-rate box workflow, and how predictable fees make roughly 300% returns possible.

lessons.title: Why Different Hosts Attract Different Buyers on Whatnot
lessons.description: Levi explains that a host's gender, age and the category they sell all affect which buyers show up. Different streamers bring in buyers the owner wouldn't reach alone, and switching categories can change who is watching and bidding.

lessons.title: How to Grow on Whatnot as a Beginner (Viewers → Buyers System)
lessons.description: Levi explains how to turn the steady stream of new viewers Whatnot sends you into buyers: welcome-ins every 5-10 minutes, explaining shipping and show notes, hyping each item, and never complaining about prices. He teaches judging profit per load instead of per item, why low-ticket items beat retail more easily, why fast sales get more algorithm traffic, and why giving buyers real deals brings them back.

lessons.title: Whatnot Shipping Guide 2026 | Bundle Shipping Explained
lessons.description: Levi explains Whatnot's USPS shipping tiers, how bundle shipping caps at $9.21 between 1 and 5 lbs, and how to use custom shipping profiles (8 oz x 10 for beauty, 15 oz x 5 for electronics) so buyers hit free shipping after two items. He also covers converting labels to large flat rate boxes, adjusting weights, and simplifying box choices so shippers can move about 1,500 units a day.

lessons.title: How We Process 2,000 Orders a Day on Whatnot (Full Warehouse Tour)
lessons.description: Six months into Whatnot, Levi tours his 2,000 sq ft warehouse and explains how he grew from two pallets in a small storage unit to eight employees. He shows his split pick-then-pack shipping process with handwritten lot numbers on each box, wheeled racks for electronics and boxes of 10 for beauty, the minimal shipping and streaming equipment you need, and why he moved single-item buyers to priority mail.

lessons.title: Why Top Whatnot Sellers Are Using The WRONG Timer
lessons.description: Levi explains how auction timer settings affect profit, viewership and the algorithm on Whatnot. He argues 5-second sudden death is too fast for custom bids and 30 seconds is too slow, and gives his recommended settings by viewer count and starting price, plus how fast to cycle inventory.

lessons.title: How I Made $500,000 on Whatnot in 6 Months
lessons.description: Levi breaks down how he went from zero to $500,000 on Whatnot in six months by hiring a team early, selling high volumes of low-cost liquidation inventory, and going live 7 hours a day across two accounts. He explains why Whatnot beats Amazon, eBay and Walmart for confident inventory investing, plus show strategies like mixing product variety and never revealing how many of an item you have.

lessons.title: Why Beginners Should Start With Pallets Instead of Truckloads
lessons.description: Levi explains that the key difference between buying pallets and truckloads is freight time and the cash it ties up. He recommends beginners with limited capital buy pallets locally and turn them over quickly, and notes the space and consistency truckload buying requires.

lessons.title: Whatnot Shipping Explained 2026 | FREE SHIPPING Strategy + Custom Profile
lessons.description: Levi breaks down Whatnot shipping: the first-class, ground, priority and flat rate tiers and their costs, which labels go on which boxes, how Whatnot shipping profiles combine in a bundle, and how custom shipping profiles with a max let you advertise offers like 'buy two, next three free shipping'. He also covers giveaway shipping at $0.78, carrier adjustments, and running big items under a small profile to get more bids.

lessons.title: How to Increase Whatnot Viewership Using Rewards Club
lessons.description: Levi explains how Whatnot's 3-month Rewards Club seasons drive viewership through notifications, and how making his tiers harder last season cut members from 2,000 to 1,000 and hurt traffic. He shares his new approach (easy first three tiers, harder top tiers, more attractive coupons) and how to price coupons by dollar amount around your average sale price while guarding against resellers making multiple accounts.

lessons.title: I Lost $100,000… Then Built a Multi-Million Dollar Whatnot Business
lessons.description: Levi tells his story from reselling on Facebook Marketplace and flipping storage units, to restaurant equipment, to seven figures on Amazon FBA, to getting shut out of eBay with $100,000 of stuck inventory that led him to Whatnot. He explains why he went all in on live social shopping: lower account risk than Amazon, about 45% net margins, and a much faster cash cycle with instant payouts.

lessons.title: How to Engage Viewers on Whatnot (Storytelling Strategy)
lessons.description: Levi argues you don't need a big personality or an expensive top streamer to sell on Whatnot; you need energy, a willingness to talk, and practice. He teaches two ways to start conversations, storytelling and asking questions, explains why chat engagement drives the algorithm, and shares how his main streamer went from worst to best by building relationships.

lessons.title: How to Sell Faster on Whatnot in 2026
lessons.description: Levi explains why fast-paced shows keep viewers on Whatnot and walks through the setup he uses to move quickly: pre-printed 2x1 number labels from a thermal printer, numbered shelves on wheels, a second phone to start auctions, and a cart flow that keeps shipping in order. He also covers organizing small beauty items in boxes of 10 and how to set auction timers for higher-ticket items.

lessons.title: How I Sold $400,000 on Whatnot in 5 Months! 2-Hour Q&A for Sellers Who Want to Scale Fast!
lessons.description: In a two-hour live Q&A, Levi answers seller questions on sourcing liquidation (local liquidators, test buys, buying at 5–20% of retail), pricing and auction speed, bundle shipping, and staffing with hourly hosts, on-demand shippers and virtual assistants. He also covers growth tactics like consistency, late-night streaming and treating every viewer as new, plus his take on warehouses, storage units, and why Whatnot beats Amazon, Walmart and eBay for resellers.

lessons.title: How To Find Inventory To Sell On Whatnot (3 Best Methods)
lessons.description: Levi covers his three best inventory sources for new Whatnot sellers: storage auctions for very low budgets, pallets from local liquidators, and online or estate auctions. He explains why to count pallet units yourself, why not to jump straight to truckloads or retailer contracts, and why he prefers liquidation over wholesale or retail arbitrage.

lessons.title: Why Selling ONLY Cheap Items on Whatnot Slows Your Business
lessons.description: Levi explains that selling only cheap, low-ticket items hurts your sell-through rate and costs more labor days, so it's better to blend in higher-ticket items. He shares how a weekly big-item show and new categories raised returning buyers, when to bring in case packs, and why to rest a product before re-running it.

lessons.title: How To Ship Whatnot Orders in 2026 (Beginner Guide)
lessons.description: Levi walks through fulfilling a Whatnot show step by step in his warehouse: printing all labels and packing slips at once on a roll thermal printer, sorting them by service, matching orders to the video receipt, and picking items on the ground into boxes. He also shows how to downgrade a big order to a large flat rate box for free, when to split boxes and pay the difference, and how to hand off to USPS with a scan sheet.

lessons.title: How I Optimized Shipping on Whatnot (7-Figure Seller Strategy)
lessons.description: Levi shares a new shipping tactic for bigger sellers: a 15 oz profile with 'buy two, next three free shipping' but no max bundle size, letting Whatnot handle ground shipping over 5 lb at roughly 45-75 cents per extra item. The money saved on out-of-pocket shipping goes into bigger $50 bundle giveaways to bring in new buyers. He contrasts this with the max-five setup he still recommends for newer sellers.

lessons.title: Whatnot Shipping Setup Explained (Priority Mail, Bundles & Box Strategy)
lessons.description: Levi breaks down the box and shipping-profile setup his team uses: order only USPS large flat rate and large shipping boxes, set priority mail in the app, and use a 71-75 oz first item plus 1 oz per added item so every buyer lands in priority mail at $9.21 with the next items free. He explains why charging the full shipping upfront improves reviews and bundle filling, how to cut down boxes, and why announcing an item count drives late-show bidding.
